question: How do I get my criminal record sealed or expunged, how long do I have to wait, and what does it cost?

groups: expungement of police and court records

gold_sections.why: Petition sealing of convictions and deferred-and-dismissed charges (misdemeanors, Class 5-6 felonies, 18.2-95 larceny): no court fees, circuit court filing, service on the Commonwealth's attorney (30 days), CCRE record, the six criteria including the 7/10-year crime-free periods, two-petition lifetime cap, excluded offenses, clerk and State Police steps.

Expungement after acquittal, nolle prosequi or dismissal (and for identity misuse): no court fees, circuit court petition, 21-day Commonwealth's attorney response, hearing, manifest-injustice standard and entitlement for a misdemeanor with no prior record; pardon and writ-of-vacatur expungements.

Separate petition route for convictions and deferred dismissals of the listed minor offenses (4.1-305 underage alcohol, misdemeanor 18.2-96/18.2-103 petit larceny and concealment, 18.2-119/120/134 trespass, misdemeanor 18.2-248.1, 18.2-265.3 A paraphernalia, 18.2-415 disorderly conduct): the court 'shall' seal once seven years have passed since conviction or deferred dismissal without a reportable conviction (no manifest-injustice finding); no fees, 30-day Commonwealth's attorney response, unlimited petitions not counted toward the 19.2-392.12 cap; ancillary matters of auto-sealed offenses.

Automatic sealing of convictions (not deferrals) for misdemeanor 18.2-96/18.2-103, 18.2-119/120/134, misdemeanor 18.2-248.1 and 18.2-415 after seven years without a new reportable conviction, unless convicted the same day of an offense not on the list; a 19.2-392.12 or 19.2-392.12:1 petition remains available.
How automatic conviction sealing happens: monthly State Police review, lists to the Executive Secretary and clerks, chief judge's order, notice back to State Police.

Misdemeanor acquittals and dismissals with prejudice are ordered automatically sealed at disposition unless the person objects; a felony acquittal or dismissal with prejudice may be sealed on an oral request with the prosecutor's concurrence; expungement remains available.
Annual automatic sealing of misdemeanor acquittals, nolle prosequis and dismissals for people with no convictions and no reportable arrests or charges in the past three years.
Former simple marijuana possession (former 18.2-250.1) charges and convictions are sealed without any court order.
What sealing does to the records held by State Police, courts and clerks, and the limited purposes for which sealed records may still be disseminated.

General deferred disposition (version effective until December 1, 2026, in force today): upon agreement of all parties a deferred dismissal, even after a plea or stipulation of facts sufficient for guilt, may be treated as 'otherwise dismissed' for expungement under 19.2-392.2, and the final order may say so.
Deferred disposition for defendants with autism or an intellectual or developmental disability: a dismissed charge may be considered 'otherwise dismissed' for expungement under 19.2-392.2.

First-offense family assault deferral: charges dismissed under it are not eligible for expungement under 19.2-392.2, and 18.2-57.3 is also on the 19.2-392.12 L.1 list of offenses ineligible for petition sealing.

Juvenile and domestic relations court records (version effective until December 1, 2026): automatic destruction once the juvenile is 19 and five years have passed since the last hearing (later for DMV-reportable offenses; felony-type findings retained), and a motion to destroy records of a charge found not guilty or dismissed; the sealing chapter applies only to adults and juveniles tried in circuit court (19.2-392.5 B).

Defines sealing and ancillary matter; effect of sealing (may deny the record to employers and agencies, with exceptions; fines and restitution still owed; no restoration of civil or firearm rights); chapter applies to adults and juveniles tried as adults.

nuggets.text: A person who was acquitted, or whose charge was nolle prossed or otherwise dismissed, may petition for expungement of the police and court records of the charge; the statute sets no waiting period.
nuggets.quote: he may file a petition setting forth the relevant facts and requesting expungement of the police records and the court records relating to the charge

nuggets.text: There are no court fees or costs for filing an expungement petition.
nuggets.quote: A person shall not be required to pay any court fees or costs for filing a petition under this subsection.

nuggets.text: After a hearing the court orders expungement if keeping and disseminating the arrest record causes or may cause a manifest injustice to the petitioner; otherwise it denies the petition.
nuggets.quote: If the court finds that the continued existence and possible dissemination of information relating to the arrest of the petitioner causes or may cause circumstances which constitute a manifest injustice to the petitioner, it shall enter an order requiring the expungement of the police and court records

nuggets.text: A petitioner with no prior criminal record whose arrest was for a misdemeanor (or whose charge was a civil offense) is entitled to expungement unless the Commonwealth shows good cause against it.
nuggets.quote: if the petitioner has no prior criminal record and the arrest was for a misdemeanor violation or the charge was for a civil offense, the petitioner shall be entitled, in the absence of good cause shown to the contrary by the Commonwealth, to expungement of the police and court records relating to the charge

nuggets.text: A person convicted of, or whose charge was deferred and dismissed for, a misdemeanor, a Class 5 or 6 felony, or felony larceny punished under 18.2-95 (offense date on or after January 1, 1986) may petition to seal the criminal history record information and court records.
nuggets.quote: a person who has been convicted of or had a charge deferred and dismissed for a (i) misdemeanor, (ii) Class 5 or 6 felony

nuggets.text: There are no court fees or costs for filing a sealing petition.
nuggets.quote: A person shall not be required to pay any court fees or costs for filing a petition pursuant to this section.

nuggets.text: The sealing petition is filed in the circuit court of the county or city where the case was disposed of.
nuggets.quote: shall be filed in the circuit court of the county or city in which the case was disposed of

nuggets.text: The petitioner sends a copy to the local attorney for the Commonwealth, who has 30 days after delivery or receipt by mail to object, answer, or give written notice of no objection.
nuggets.quote: The attorney for the Commonwealth may file an objection or answer to the petition or may give written notice to the court that he does not object to the petition within 30 days after it is delivered to him or received in the mail.

nuggets.text: Waiting period for petition sealing: no new reportable conviction (traffic infractions excluded) for seven years for a misdemeanor or ten years for a felony.
nuggets.quote: Seven years for any misdemeanor offense; or b. Ten years for any felony offense

nuggets.text: The waiting period runs from the latest of dismissal of the deferred charge, conviction, release from incarceration, or a later probation or suspended-sentence violation finding or release from incarceration for it.
nuggets.quote: During a period after the date of (i) dismissal of a deferred charge, (ii) conviction, (iii) release from incarceration on the charge or conviction set forth in the petition, (iv) a finding that the person was in violation of a suspended sentence, probation, or parole related to the charge or conviction set forth in the petition, or (v) release from incarceration following a finding that the person was in violation of a suspended sentence, probation, or parole related to the charge or conviction set forth in the petition, whichever date occurred later

nuggets.text: Any restitution ordered for the charge or conviction must be paid in full before it can be sealed.
nuggets.quote: If the petitioner was ordered by a court to pay restitution as a condition of any charge, conviction, or ancillary matter that is the subject of the petition, such restitution has been paid in full

nuggets.text: The circuit court orders sealing only if it finds all six statutory criteria are met (felony history limits, crime-free period, rehabilitation where drugs or alcohol were involved, restitution paid, no two prior sealings, and manifest injustice).
nuggets.quote: The court shall enter an order requiring the sealing of the criminal history record information and court records, including electronic records, related to the charge or conviction, only if the court finds that all criteria in subdivisions 1 through 6 are met

nuggets.text: A person may have only two sealing petitions under 19.2-392.12 granted in a lifetime.
nuggets.quote: A petitioner may only have two petitions granted pursuant to this section within his lifetime.

nuggets.text: Many offenses are ineligible for petition sealing under 19.2-392.12, including DUI, sex-offender-registry offenses, violent felonies, protective-order violations and crimes against a family or household member; some bars last only while a condition holds (a firearm felony until firearm rights are restored, animal-related offenses while the companion-animal prohibition or dog ownership continues).
nuggets.quote: The following offenses are ineligible for sealing under this section

nuggets.text: Convictions (not deferrals) for the listed minor offenses (misdemeanor petit larceny or concealment, trespass, misdemeanor 18.2-248.1 marijuana offenses, disorderly conduct) are usually sealed automatically after seven years with no new reportable conviction; not if the person was convicted the same day of an offense not on the list.
nuggets.quote: Subject to the provisions of subsection C, any conviction listed under subsection A shall be ordered to be automatically sealed if seven years have passed since the date of the conviction

nuggets.text: A person convicted of, or with a charge deferred and dismissed for, a listed minor offense (also underage alcohol under 4.1-305 and paraphernalia under 18.2-265.3 A) may petition, and the court must seal once seven years have passed since the conviction or deferred dismissal with no new reportable conviction; no manifest-injustice finding is needed.
nuggets.quote: the court shall enter an order requiring the sealing of the records related to the charge, conviction, or ancillary matter if the court finds that seven years have passed since the date of conviction or of dismissal of the deferred charge

nuggets.text: There is no limit on the number of 19.2-392.12:1 petitions granted, and they do not count toward the two-petition lifetime cap of 19.2-392.12.
nuggets.quote: A petitioner is not limited in the number of petitions that may be granted pursuant to this section within his lifetime.

nuggets.text: There are no court fees or costs for filing a 19.2-392.12:1 petition.
nuggets.quote: A person shall not be required to pay any court fees or costs for filing a petition pursuant to this section.

nuggets.text: Felony-history bar for petition sealing: never convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or a life felony, no Class 3 or 4 felony conviction in the past 20 years, and no other felony conviction in the past 10 years, counted back from the filing date.
nuggets.quote: never been convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or any other felony punishable by imprisonment for life, (ii) not been convicted of a Class 3 or 4 felony within the past 20 years, and (iii) not been convicted of any other felony within the past 10 years from the date the petition was filed

nuggets.text: When a misdemeanor charge (not a traffic infraction) ends in acquittal or dismissal with prejudice, the court orders it automatically sealed at disposition unless the person objects.
nuggets.quote: the court disposing of the matter shall order that the charge be automatically sealed under the process described in § 19.2-392.13 , unless the person charged with the offense objects to such automatic sealing

nuggets.text: After a felony acquittal or dismissal with prejudice, the person may orally ask right away for sealing, and with the prosecutor's concurrence the court orders it.
nuggets.quote: Upon such request and with the concurrence of the attorney for the Commonwealth, the court shall order the automatic sealing of records relating to the arrest or charge

nuggets.text: At least once a year the State Police identify misdemeanor acquittals, nolle prosequis and dismissals (not deferred dismissals) of people with no reportable convictions and no reportable arrests or charges in the past three years, for automatic sealing.
nuggets.quote: On at least an annual basis, the Department of State Police shall electronically review the Central Criminal Records Exchange and identify all persons with finalized misdemeanor case dispositions

nuggets.text: A charge dismissed after a general deferred disposition can be treated as 'otherwise dismissed', and so expunged rather than sealed, if all parties agree (the final order may say so); deferrals for autism or intellectual disability under 19.2-303.6 can be treated the same way.
nuggets.quote: Upon agreement of all parties, a charge that is dismissed pursuant to this section, including an original charge that was reduced or a charge that is dismissed after a plea or stipulation of the facts that would justify a finding of guilt, may be considered as otherwise dismissed for purposes of expungement of police and court records

nuggets.text: A first-offense family assault charge dismissed after deferral under 18.2-57.3 cannot be expunged (and 18.2-57.3 is also ineligible for petition sealing).
nuggets.quote: No charges dismissed pursuant to this section shall be eligible for expungement under

nuggets.text: The expungement petition is filed in the circuit court of the county or city where the case ended in acquittal or dismissal.
nuggets.quote: shall be filed in the circuit court of the county or city in which the case was disposed of by acquittal or being otherwise dismissed

nuggets.text: The petition is served on the attorney for the Commonwealth, who has 21 days after service to object, answer or give written notice of no objection.
nuggets.quote: The attorney for the Commonwealth may file an objection or answer to the petition or may give written notice to the court that he does not object to the petition within 21 days after it is served on him.

nuggets.text: Sealing does not cancel any fines, costs, forfeitures, penalties or restitution owed for the offense (petition sealing under 19.2-392.12 additionally needs restitution paid in full first).
nuggets.quote: shall not relieve the person who was arrested, charged, or convicted of any obligation to pay all fines, costs, forfeitures, penalties, or restitution in relation to the offense that was ordered to be sealed

answer:
Not convicted. After an acquittal, nolle prosequi or dismissal, petition the circuit court where the case ended to expunge the records [N1][N25], with no waiting period [N1]. The prosecutor gets 21 days [N26]. The judge expunges for manifest injustice [N3], and must for a misdemeanor arrest with no prior record, absent good cause [N4]. Misdemeanor acquittals and dismissals with prejudice are also sealed automatically unless you object [N20]; felony ones on an immediate request if the prosecutor agrees [N21]. A deferred-disposition dismissal counts for expungement if all parties agree [N23]; family-assault deferrals never do [N24].

Convicted, or deferred and dismissed. For a misdemeanor, Class 5 or 6 felony, or felony larceny dated on or after January 1, 1986 [N5], petition that court to seal [N7] after 7 years (misdemeanor) or 10 (felony) without a new reportable conviction [N9], counted from the latest of dismissal, conviction, release, or a later probation or parole violation finding or release [N10]. You need no Class 1 or 2 felony ever, no Class 3 or 4 felony in 20 years, no other felony in 10 [N19], restitution paid [N11], and manifest injustice [N12]. The prosecutor gets 30 days [N8]. Two grants per lifetime [N13]; many offenses are ineligible [N14].

Listed minor convictions (petit larceny, trespass, disorderly conduct) are usually sealed automatically after 7 years [N15]; otherwise the court must seal them on petition [N16], without lifetime limit [N17].

Cost: no court fees for any petition [N2][N6][N18], but fines, costs and restitution remain owed [N27].

gaps: The petition steps are drawn in sequence for soundness: in law the Commonwealth's attorney's 30 days run from delivery or mailing of the copy (19.2-392.12 D) while the CCRE request (E) proceeds in parallel; the court acts 'after receiving the criminal history record' (F).

A hearing is permissive (F: 'may conduct a hearing'); G lets the court enter the order without one when the Commonwealth's attorney gives written notice of no objection and stipulates that the petitioner is eligible and that the record causes or may cause a manifest injustice. The hearing_held condition summarizes this. The statute states no consequence if the attorney for the Commonwealth does not respond within 30 days (the deadline's consequence is 'unstated'); routing a missed response to the hearing is a modelling choice, made because the no-hearing route in G needs the written no-objection notice and stipulation.

H lets any party aggrieved by the decision appeal, so the attorney for the Commonwealth may appeal a sealing order just as the petitioner may appeal a denial; the appeal step is drawn in the petitioner's lane only because a step has one actor. Its 30-day window comes from E (the court destroys the criminal history record after the hearing unless the petitioner or the attorney for the Commonwealth notes an appeal within 30 days of the final order); the time and manner of noting a civil appeal are set by court rule.

Eligibility (A, L) and the six findings (F.1-F.6) are summarized in the sealing_criteria table. Rehabilitation (F.3) is required only when the records show the occurrence involved alcohol or drugs; the table treats that input as true when it does not apply.

One petition may cover several charges only if they arose from the same transaction or occurrence (ancillary matters such as probation violations, contempt and failure to appear may be added); only two petitions may be granted in a lifetime (C).
The petition and the Commonwealth's attorney's pleadings stay under seal (K); an order entered without strict compliance or contrary to law is voidable on motion within two years (J).

Expungement of acquittals, nolle prosequis and dismissals (19.2-392.2) is a separate petition with a 21-day Commonwealth's attorney response, a hearing unless the Commonwealth's attorney does not object (and, for a felony, stipulates manifest injustice), and removal of the records through the State Police; it is not modelled here.

Automatic routes need no petition: listed minor convictions after seven years (19.2-392.6, monthly under 19.2-392.7), misdemeanor acquittals and dismissals with prejudice at disposition unless the person objects (19.2-392.8, notified monthly to the State Police under 19.2-392.10), annual sealing of misdemeanor non-convictions for people with no convictions and no reportable charges in three years (19.2-392.11), and former marijuana possession (19.2-392.6:1). Automatic conviction sealing fails if the person was convicted the same day of an offense not on the list (19.2-392.6 C), and the State Police need not list an offense whose eligibility electronic review cannot decide or where the person was charged out of state in the seven years (19.2-392.7 B); the fallback is a 19.2-392.12:1 petition, under which the court must seal after seven years and which does not count toward the two-petition limit.

Deferred dismissals sit between the tracks: they are normally sealed by petition under 19.2-392.12 after the 7- or 10-year wait, but a 19.2-298.02 or 19.2-303.6 dismissal may be treated as 'otherwise dismissed' and expunged under 19.2-392.2 with no wait (for 19.2-298.02, upon agreement of all parties), while an 18.2-57.3 family-assault deferral can be neither expunged (18.2-57.3 E) nor sealed by petition (19.2-392.12 L.1).

version_flags: 19.2-392.2 is the version effective until December 1, 2026 (in force on 2026-10-10); the version taking effect December 1, 2026 is not in the downloaded corpus.

19.2-392.6 A and 19.2-392.12:1 A: the text effective until July 1, 2027 is in force (it lists a misdemeanor violation of 18.2-248.1); the version effective July 1, 2027 refers to former 18.2-248.1, which is headed 'Repeal effective July 1, 2027'.
9.1-134 (sealing procedures cited throughout the chapter) is headed 'Effective until July 1, 2026', so it has expired; the version in force after that date is not in the downloaded corpus.
16.1-306 (expungement of juvenile court records) and 19.2-298.02 (deferred disposition) are versions effective until December 1, 2026; their replacements are not in the corpus.
19.2-392.12:2 requires annual sealing-petition data reports beginning October 1, 2027.
local_option: None in the statutes: eligibility, waiting periods and fees are statewide. Only the local attorney for the Commonwealth's choice to object, or to consent and stipulate (which lets the court rule without a hearing), varies by city or county.
notes: Virginia has two petition remedies in circuit court, both free of court fees and costs: expungement (19.2-392.2) for acquittals, nolle prosequis and dismissals (also identity misuse, absolute pardons and writs of vacatur), with no statutory waiting period; and sealing (19.2-392.12) for convictions and deferred-and-dismissed charges of misdemeanors, Class 5 or 6 felonies and 18.2-95 larceny, after 7 (misdemeanor) or 10 (felony) years without a reportable conviction, with restitution paid, a felony-history bar (no Class 1 or 2 or life felony ever, no Class 3 or 4 felony in 20 years, no other felony in 10 years before filing: F.1), a two-petition lifetime cap and a long list of offenses ineligible for petition sealing (L, e.g., DUI 18.2-266, sex-registry offenses, violent felonies, protective-order violations, offenses against a family or household member; L.4, L.13 and L.14 lapse when firearm rights are restored or the animal prohibition or dog ownership ends). Listed minor offenses can be sealed by an unlimited, mandatory 19.2-392.12:1 petition after 7 years (that list adds 4.1-305 underage alcohol and 18.2-265.3 A paraphernalia and covers deferred dismissals) and their convictions are also sealed automatically (19.2-392.6/.7). Deferred dismissals under 19.2-298.02 (on agreement of all parties) and 19.2-303.6 may be expunged as 'otherwise dismissed'; 18.2-57.3 family-assault deferrals may not (18.2-57.3 E). Misdemeanor acquittals and dismissals with prejudice are sealed automatically at disposition unless the person objects (19.2-392.8) and in an annual sweep for people with no convictions (19.2-392.11); former marijuana possession is sealed without an order (19.2-392.6:1); non-criminal traffic infractions are deemed sealed after 11 years (19.2-392.17). The only fee-like items in the statutes: police may charge up to $10 for the first card and $5 for each additional card for fingerprints voluntarily requested for non-criminal purposes (19.2-392 B, not a gold section), which may apply to the fingerprint set an identity-misuse expungement needs (19.2-392.2 B, E); no fee to move to see one's own sealed court record (19.2-392.13 D). Sealing does not cancel fines, costs or restitution, or restore civil or firearm rights (19.2-392.5 F, K); the chapter covers adults and juveniles tried in circuit court (19.2-392.5 B); juvenile court records follow 16.1-306. Employers, schools, landlords, insurers and licensing agencies may not require disclosure of sealed records (19.2-392.15, with exceptions) or expunged records (19.2-392.4); these effect-of-relief sections and the 19.2-392.10 notification step are left out of gold because the answer does not rest on them.
